en: Now, for the sake of success, having first bowed to Vāgīśvarī, whose beautiful luster is like a fresh lotus, [the author] Śrī Āśubodhavidyābhūṣaṇa,
elucidating the instruction on words in clear and simple speech, composes this commentary, the Sāramañjarī.
The wise Viprāśubodha, honored by the name Śeṣa-Vidyābhūṣaṇa, explains this "Mañjarī," which begins with the word "Sāra" and was composed by Jayakṛṣṇasūri.

Indeed, grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is the instruction of words (*śabdānuśāsana*), according to the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "Now, the instruction of words. Furthermore, the worthiness of the words of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) is well-established from Vedic passages such as: "A single word, well-employed and correctly understood, becomes a cow of plenty (*kāmadhuk*) in the heavenly world."

In this regard, since it is the essential core of grammar alone that governs the understanding of the application of words, the author Tarkālaṅkāra—desiring to compose a work titled *Sāramañjarī* for the easy comprehension of those of delicate intellect who wish to know the complete system of grammatical tenets—performs an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) consisting of a salutation to Vināyaka, the destroyer of obstacles, which is the object of the undisputed conduct of the learned. Desiring the unimpeded completion of his intended work, he says "praṇamya" (having bowed).

Having bowed to the pair of feet of Lord Heramba, who utterly destroys all obstacles, this *Sāramañjarī*—the essence of the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*), as the word "of" (*iti śeṣaḥ*) implies—is being composed by Jayakṛṣṇa Śarman, who holds the title of Tarkālaṅkāra, just as a cluster of blossoms (*mañjarī*) is described.

Therein, at the outset, he defines time itself as the regulator of all things, beginning with the words "Among these... (*tatra*). Among those things to be defined, although time is indivisible, its threefold nature—as past, present, and future—is logically established through the distinctions of the objects residing within it.

"Varttamāne" and so forth. The meaning is "having as its counter-positive the destruction belonging to the present time," which is to say, "that which has begun but not yet been completed. That past time is indeed twofold, distinguished as "adyatana" (belonging to today) and "anadyatana" (not belonging to today). That time which is comprised of the latter half of the past night together with the former half of the coming night is the "adyatana-past," being the counter-positive of a destruction occurring therein; that which is other than this is "anadyatana. "Varttamāna" means "having the property of arising after the time of the present."

Regarding the phrase *svāvacchinna* and so forth: its meaning is either "simultaneity with the time of the [verbal] usage" or "having been commenced but not yet completed. That object by which a time is delimited is the "present" (*varttamāna*) of that [object]; for example, in the expression "now the jar exists," the jar is present. Furthermore, it is divided into four types, as follows: "The present is of four kinds: that which has begun but ceased, that which has occurred and not yet ceased, that which is eternally occurring, and that which is proximate (*sāmīpya*)."

Thus, the examples of these [types of negation] in sequence are as follows: "He does not eat meat"—this is understood as one who was previously engaged in eating meat but has subsequently desisted from it. In the case of "The boys are playing here," even though there is no play at that present moment, it is because previous plays are present in the mind.

Mountains exist because they are eternally active; furthermore, although mountains exist in the present by virtue of their stability, one may say "the mountains stood" or "the mountains will stand" when there is an intention to express a connection with the past or future times. Moreover, proximity is of two kinds: proximity to the past and proximity to the future.

Regarding proximity to the present (*bhūtasāmīpya*): for example, when asked "When did you arrive?", even though one has already arrived, because the fatigue from the journey and so forth is still present, one says, "Here I am coming. Regarding proximity to the future (*bhaviṣyatsāmīpya*): for example, when asked "When will you go?", while the effort for going is currently being made, one says, "Here I am going."

Now, regarding the passage beginning with *atheti*: after the determination of the three divisions of time (*kālatraya*), [the author] next determines the expressive power (*śakti*) of the verbal suffixes (*laṭ* etc. which denote specific times. Indeed, there are ten kinds of *lakāras*: *laṭ*, *liṭ*, *luṭ*, *lṛṭ*, *leṭ*, and *loṭ*—these six ending in *ṭ*; and *laṅ*, *liṅ*, *luṅ*, and *lṛṅ*—these four ending in *ṅ*. Tarkālaṅkāra clearly provides examples of their specific points of usage. On this matter, Hari says: "In the present, in the remote past, in the sense of what will happen tomorrow, and in the future..."

"The *laṭ* and other [suffixes] are to be known as used respectively for injunction (*vidhi*), request (*prārthanā*), and so forth; likewise, the *laṭ* and others are used for the past day (*hyo bhūte*), instigation (*preraṇā*), and simple past (*bhūtamātra*). Furthermore, when there is the non-occurrence of an action (*kriyātipatti*), the *lṛṅ* is prescribed for both the past and the future. (Kārikā 2) Regarding "injunction" (*vidhi*): the author of the *Bhāṣya* states that injunction means "commanding" (*preṣaṇa*). Its meaning is the directing of someone, such as a servant, toward a particular action. For example: "One who desires heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice. (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.9.1)

Regarding "liṭ" and so forth: the meaning of *liṭ* is the past tense not belonging to the current day (*anadyatana-bhūtatva*) and remoteness (*pārokṣya*). Remoteness (*pārokṣya*), however, means being outside the range of the sense organs such as the eyes—that is to say, being an object distinct from direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*). For this reason, the suffix *liṭ* is not employed when the action has been directly perceived. Now, one might ask: how can *liṭ* apply in cases such as "I cooked" (*ahaṃ papāca*), where the first person is used? Regarding this, the ancients have stated that it is due to a distraction of the mind (*cittavyāsaṅga*). Consequently, the resulting meaning is that [the action] is not an object of knowledge such as "I am perceiving it directly" (*sākṣāt karomi*).

Regarding *lṛṅ*: its meaning consists of pastness (*bhūtatva*), futurity (*bhaviṣyatva*), and the relation between producer and produced (*janya-janakatva*), according to the rule "When there is a condition for the optative (*liṅ*), *lṛṅ* is used for the non-occurrence of the action" (Pāṇini 3.3.139).

Regarding "yaṅ" and so forth: the intensification (*samabhihāra*) of an action means either repetition (*paunaḥpunya*) or intensity (*bhṛśārtha*). In this regard, there is this distinction: repetition applies to principal actions, while intensity applies to those factors that assist the principal action, such as placing [the pot] on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) and so on. For instance, in the case of *pāpacyate*, it is understood as "he cooks again and again," and not as "he cooks intensely," because [intensity] pertains to the very nature of the principal action itself.

In the expression *jājvalyate*, it is appropriate to understand it as "it blazes intensely," and not as "it blazes again and again," because [the prefix *ā*] serves to assist the primary action (*pradhānakriyā*).

Now, regarding the word *atha*: that object which is apprehended by the sense of hearing is *śabda* (sound). Furthermore, it is of two kinds: consisting of *dhvani* (phonation/noise) and consisting of *varṇa* (articulated phonemes). Of these, the former is well-known in the case of a kettle-drum (*bherī*) and so forth; the latter consists of the nature of languages such as *saṃskṛta*. Here, indeed, the term *śābdabodha* means this comprehension or understanding of a word in the form of the *saṃskṛta* language; that is to say, it refers to the mode of understanding the syntactic connection (*anvaya*).

Regarding the phrase *vākyārtha* (sentence-meaning): a sentence (*vākya*) is indeed a collection of words that serves as the means for producing a cognition whose primary object is a single qualificand consisting of an action conjoined with its factors (*kārakas*). And it has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*: "A sentence is said to be that which has expectant parts, which does not expect other words when its own distinctions are complete, which has action as its primary element, which possesses a single meaning, and which is endowed with qualities. (*Vākyapadīya* 2.3) The meaning of such a sentence is precisely its *tātparyārtha* (intended meaning).

Nor is "intention" (tātparya) defined as the speaker's desire, because it would be impossible for there to be comprehension of meaning in the case of the Veda and similar texts uttered by a person who lacks knowledge of their meaning, or in the case of verses recited by parrots and the like. For this very reason, it has been said that intention is the capacity to generate the cognition of that [meaning].

That too is not correct; for if that were the case, when it is instructed in the context of eating, "One should bring *saindhava*," there would follow the undesirable consequence of bringing both salt and a horse simultaneously, since the word *saindhava* is equally capable of conveying both meanings. How, then, is its determination achieved? It is as follows: *tātparya* (intentionality) is the capacity to produce the cognition of a particular meaning, provided that the word has not been uttered with the desire to produce the cognition of any other [meaning].

Now, "atha" [introduces the following]: Transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*) are indeed of two kinds: those with one object (*ekakarmaka*) and those with two objects (*dvikarmaka*). Verbs such as *gam* (to go) and others, which convey a meaning associated with a single object, are "one-object" verbs. As for the two-object verbs, they are of two types: those whose meaning consists of a single operation associated with two objects, and those whose meaning consists of two operations associated with two objects.

Among these, the first group consists of roots such as *duh* (to milk), and according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), they do not have two operations (*vyāpāra*) as their meaning. If that were the case, it would be possible for both operations to connect with only the two objects (*karman*)—namely, those most desired (*īpsitatama*)—and consequently, when the accusative and other cases arise, it would be inappropriate to prescribe the technical designation "object" (*karma-saṃjñā*) for the root *duh* and others by the rule "akathitaṃ ca" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.51), since that rule applies to a factor that has not already received another technical designation. On the other hand, causative forms (*ṇijanta*) whose meanings involve two operations connected to two objects are verbal roots (*dhātu*) that possess only a single object.

In that context, one operation (vyāpāra) is expressed by the verbal root (dhātu), while the second is expressed by the causative suffix (ṇic). Furthermore, the desired object (īpsita-karman) and the object in the form of the instigating agent (prayojaka-kartṛ-karman) are connected respectively to these two operations. It should be understood that this is the case for verbs such as *gam* (to go) and others. However, it is not so for other [verbs], because when they are joined [with a causal suffix], the instigating agent does not receive the technical designation "object" (karma-saṃjñā); consequently, there is no connection of two objects with the two operations.

Regarding the term *akathitam*: that *kāraka* which is not intended to be designated by specific technical names such as *apādāna* (ablative) and so forth shall receive the designation *karman* (object). This is according to the rule *akathitaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.51). This prescription of the *karman* designation is for the purpose of obtaining the second case ending (*dvitīyā*).

Regarding the word *carmaṇi*: Durga states, "When there is a connection with an action (*karma-saṃyoga*), the locative case may optionally be used after a cause (*nimitta*). By this rule, the meaning understood is "on the hide," that is, "on account of the hide. Here, a "cause" (*nimitta*) refers to the fruit of an action; if, however, it were said to mean a "material cause" (*kāraṇa*), then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "bound by dullness" (*jāḍyena baddhaḥ*). Furthermore, "connection" (*saṃyoga*) here takes the form of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), or other types of relations. Among these, between the leopard's skin and the boundary of the musk deer, there is inherence (*samavāya*), because of the relationship of part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*).

Haradatta, however, says that *puṣyalaka* is a *śaṅku* (stake) driven into the boundary for the purpose of knowing the boundary. According to this view, there is a conjunction between the boundary and the *puṣyalaka*. In examples such as *muktāphalāya kariṇam* (an elephant for the sake of pearls) and *hariṇam palāya* (a deer for the sake of fleeing), the dative case is used by the rule *kriyārthopapadasya* (Pāṇini 2.3.14), with the intended meaning being "to fetch pearls. Many scholars maintain that this is simply a grammatical error (*apaprayoga*).
It should be understood that this rule prohibits the third case (*tṛtīyā*) in the sense of cause (*hetu*) and the fourth case (*caturthī*) in the sense of purpose (*tādarthya*).

Regarding the term *satī*: the locative case (*saptamī*) used here is the so-called "locative of condition" (*sati-saptamī*), prescribed by the rule "yas‍ya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam" (Pāṇini 2.3.37). In this context, the meaning of the locative is that of a delimiter characterized by identity of place and time. Therefore, in examples such as ‘goṣu duhyamānāsu āgata’ ("he arrived while the cows were being milked"), the locative is applied to the cows and so forth, because the time of his arrival is delimited by the time of the action of milking the cows.

In cases such as "guṇe sati dravyatvam asti" ("when there is quality, substantiality exists"), it should be understood that the seventh case ending occurs after the word denoting the quality (*guṇa*), because the existence of the quality delimits the locus of the existence of substantiality. It is well known that an action whose time and place are already determined serves to delimit the time and place of an action whose time and place are not yet determined; and this [delimiting function] occurs sometimes by means of a time coeval with itself, and sometimes by means of times preceding or following it. By this principle, the grammatical correctness is established in examples such as "dugdhāsu goṣu" ("when the cows have been milked") and "dhokṣyamāṇāsu goṣu" ("when the cows are about to be milked").

Now, regarding the term *atheti*: being a *kāraka* (participant in action) consists in possessing the power to produce an action (*kriyājanaka-śaktimattva*). This is because the *Bhāṣya* shows the etymological derivation as "it performs (*karoti*) the action, it brings it about," and because the *Vārttika* states: "That which is effective (*sādhaka*), i.e., that which accomplishes an action, is designated as a *kāraka*. Furthermore, there is another view according to which the status of being a *kāraka* belongs to the action itself, since power alone exists through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the action. As stated by Bhartṛhari: "Just as [powers] inherent in their own substratum [are perceived], so too [they are perceived] in another substratum..."

"They know that the capacity for the accomplishment of actions is the *sādhana* (means). It should be understood that because there is no difference between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), the conventional usage refers to the substance (*dravya*) as the *kāraka*. Thus, although all [factors] possess the status of agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of being generators of action, their status as instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth is to be understood solely through the intention to express their respective internal operations (*vyāpāra*). Regarding this, it was said by Hari: "The status of agent exists in every *kāraka* simply in respect to the mere production [of the action]."

"When there is a requirement for a distinction in function, the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) and so forth becomes possible. (3) Herein, the inclusion of internal distinctions is as follows: the function of the agent (*kartṛ*) is the act of instigating other factors of action (*kāraka*); the function of the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the immediate operation that produces the action; the function of the object (*karman*) is the state of being intended as the goal through the fruit of the action; the function of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the supporting of the action mediated by the agent and the object; the function of the recipient (*sampradāna*) is the operation of instigation, consent, and so forth;
and the function of the point of departure (*apādāna*) is the state of being a limit and the operation of separation.

Regarding the phrase *maitrasya*: it is clear that [the word] *maitra*, which is related to the rice (*taṇḍula*), lacks the status of a *kāraka* because it does not directly connect with the action expressed by "cooks" (*pacati*), according to the previously stated definition that being a *kāraka* consists in being connected with an action.

Regarding the term *kartṛ* (agent): agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in being the substratum of an operation denoted by a verbal root (*dhātu*). As stated by Hari: "An agent is always intended as that factor (*kāraka*) whose action is expressed by the verbal root. This [agent] is of two kinds, distinguished as the independent (*svatantra*) and the prompter (*tatprayojaka*). Among these, independence (*svātantrya*) consists in possessing an operation that is not dependent on the operations of others, or in possessing an operation that prompts other factors (*kārakas*). Regarding this, Hari says: "Prior to obtaining power from another, and prior even to the production of existence..."

"Because the activity of those who have begun [an action] depends upon it, because it causes them to desist, because no substitute is observed for it, because it is seen in isolation, and because it assists from afar, the independence of the agent is maintained. (2)

This is its meaning: because even during the operation of other factors, one's own operation exists; because other causal factors (kārakas) are seen to have their activity and cessation dependent on themselves, whereas for the agent (kartṛ)—like an axe for a woodcutter—there is no possibility of a substitute; because even when other causal factors are not employed, the word denoting the agent itself is used; and because the agent possesses an operation that directly produces the result conveyed by the verbal root (dhātu), the agent possesses independence (svātantrya).

Even in cases such as *pācayati* ("he causes to cook"), the prompted agent (*prayojya*) indeed possesses independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to the act of cooking, because his engagement [in the activity] is solely for the sake of achieving his own purpose, namely the acquisition of wages and the like.

Regarding the term "action" (*kriyā*): this action, expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*), consists of both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*), or rather, it is characterized by those two; for there is the traditional saying of the venerable ones: "The verbal root denotes both the result and the operation. On this point, Hari has also stated: "The operation is *bhāvanā*; that itself is production (*utpādanā*), and that itself is action (*kriyā*). Furthermore: "Whatever is perceived as being in the process of accomplishment—whether already established or not yet established—"

"Because its nature consists of a sequence of dependent stages, it is designated as 'action' (kriyā). The meaning is that what is established is the past time, which is the counter-correlative of the destruction of the present; that which is different from that is the unestablished, namely the present and the future. Thus, the intention is that by this [definition], the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the word "action" is demonstrated as referring to "action" in all instances—such as *apacat* (he cooked), *pakṣyati* (he will cook), and *pacati* (he cooks)—as being that which is to be accomplished and whose nature is non-existence.

"Fivefold": because that action (*kriyā*) consists of one among the five types of actions whose essential natures are distinguished by varieties such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*), downward throwing (*apakṣepaṇa*), and so forth; and because it has the nature of a specific action (*karmaviśeṣa*), it is said that while [the action] resides in the agent (*kartṛsthatva*), those [other factors] distinct from it reside in the object (*karmasthatva*). "The state of being an object" (*karmatva*): the meaning is that it is the state of possessing a result (*phala*) produced by the action that is non-co-referential (*vyadhikaraṇa*) with it; or alternatively, the state of being an object is the state of being desired to be connected with a result brought about by the agent's own inherent activity (*vyāpāra*).

"Of three kinds," and so forth. Regarding this, it was stated by Hari (Bhartṛhari): "It is considered to be of three types: that which is to be produced (*nirvartya*), that which is to be modified (*vikārya*), and that which is to be reached (*prāpya*). Furthermore, that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*) is the [primary] object (*karman*); another fourfold classification has been devised: that which is obtained through indifference (*audāsīnyena*), and that which is not desired by the agent (*anīpsita*)."

Having stated the different varieties [of action] with such words as, "That which is not designated by other names, and that which is preceded by something else," he provides the definitions and examples for *nirvartya* (that which is produced) and the others: "That which is born as non-existent, or that which manifests through birth, is the *nirvartya*; and the *vikārya* (that which is modified) is established in two ways. One arises from the destruction of the material cause (*prakṛti*), like the ashes of wood and so forth; the other arises from the production of a new quality (*guṇāntara*), like the modification of gold and so forth."

"Where the accomplishment of specific qualities produced by an action is not apprehended through either perception or inference, that [object] is said to be 'to-be-attained' (*prāpya*). (Verse 2) Regarding "to-be-attained": *Prāpyatva* is the state of being intended as the goal by virtue of possessing a result produced by an action, while not being the locus of a cognition whose mode is a common property produced by that action. For example, in cases such as "he goes to the village," the village and so forth are such [objects]. This is because the result in the form of conjunction, residing in the locus of the action, is common [to both the agent and the object], whereas uncommon results such as origination (*utpatti*) do not exist there; thus it possesses that [status of being *prāpya*]. Thus [ends the explanation].

Regarding the term *nirvartyam* (that which is produced): *nirvartyatva* (the state of being produced) consists in having as its result an origination (*utpatti*) brought about by an action, while being presented by a word that is not co-occurrent with a word denoting a material cause (*prakṛti*). Origination (*utpatti*) is either of the nature of a connection with the first moment, or of the nature of a first manifestation, as stated in the passage beginning with "that which was non-existent" (*yadasat*). Furthermore, as stated in: "Whether the material cause (*prakṛti*) is already existent or merely present, when it is not relied upon [as the substrate], one declares that [object] to be *nirvartya*," the phrase "denoting a material cause" (*prakṛtivācaka*) and so forth is employed.

For instance, in cases such as "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), the jar is the object; and in cases such as "she gives birth to a son" (*putraṃ prasūte*), the son and so forth are the objects. Regarding the term *vikārya* (the object of transformation): the state of being a *vikārya* consists in possessing one of two types of results—either the production of a specific non-existence (*asattva*) brought about by the action, or the manifestation of a state of being a modification (*vikṛti*) in relation to a perceived material cause (*prakṛti*). For example, in "he makes gold into an earring" (*suvarṇaṃ kuṇḍalaṃ karoti*), the gold and the earring are the objects. Here, this status [of being a *vikārya*] exists because the gold possesses the result consisting of the non-existence of its previous form, and because the earring possesses the result consisting of its own production.

It should be understood that, according to the definition stated by Hari, the production of an earring (*kuṇḍala*) from gold occurs through the imposition of certain other qualities [upon the gold]. Likewise, this applies to cases such as "he turns wood into ash," where the same principle holds for the wood, the ash, and so forth. The distinction here is that in such cases, the wood possesses destruction—which is characterized by a specific non-existence produced by an action—and thus it is so designated. For, according to Hari’s definition, it is understood that the production of ash occurs through the cessation of the wood's substrate (*prakṛti*).

"Thus," and so forth. The aforementioned triad is the "most desired" (*īpsitatama*) because it is that which the agent aims at most intensely through the fruit of the action. That which is distinct from this is conceived as fourfold; the meaning is that these are technical (*pāribhāṣika*) [karmas]. And those are: the indifferent (*udāsīna*), the two types of the "unexpressed" (*akathita*), and the "non-precedent" (*apūrvaka*). Among these, indifference (*udāsīnatva*) consists in being possessed of a fruit produced by the action while not being intended by the agent.

For example, in such cases as "while going to the village, he touches grass," although the grass and so forth lack the status of being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*), they possess that status because they possess a conjunction produced by the action. The state of being an object of aversion (*dveṣyatva*) consists in possessing a result produced by the action while being a means to what is disliked; for example, in such cases as "one desiring to eat food eats poison," the poison and so forth [are objects of aversion].

Furthermore, there is the "unspoken" (akathita) object; that is to say, when—due to the lack of desire to express it by any other specific technical designation of a *kāraka*—it functions as an auxiliary to the object (*karman*), it possesses the status of being "unspoken. For example, in such cases as "he milks the cow for milk" (*gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ*), the cow and so forth possess that status because they are useful for the milk and because their status as any other *kāraka* is not intended to be expressed. This and similar points should be understood through careful discernment.

Regarding the term "therein" (*tatra*): that which is intended as the most excellent (*prakṛṣṭa*) auxiliary factor (*upakāraka*) for the accomplishment of an action (*kriyā*), being an internal factor (*antaraṅga*), is the instrument (*karaṇa*). It is "most excellent" because the production of the result occurs immediately following its operation; this is understood from the suffix *-tama* in the sūtra, which conveys excellence in the form of having an uninterrupted operation. As stated by Bhartṛhari:

"When the accomplishment of an action is intended to be expressed as occurring immediately after a particular operation, that [operation] is then remembered as the *karaṇa* (instrument) in that context. By the word "is intended" (*vivakṣyate*) here, it is indicated that even other *kārakas* (grammatical factors) may possess the status of an instrument. This too was stated by Bhartṛhari: "In reality, that [instrument] cannot be definitively specified, for it is not fixed as a thing-in-itself; since the usage 'it is cooked in a pot' (*sthālyā pacyate*) is observed. Here, the "thing" (*vastu*) refers to the category of the instrument (*karaṇapadārtha*). Thus it is said.

Regarding the term *sampradānatva* (the state of being a recipient): it means the status of being intended as the locus for the possession of a result produced by the action. And that [status] is threefold: the non-rejecting (*anirākartṛ*), the instigator (*preraka*), and the consenter (*anumantṛ*). As stated by Bhartṛhari: "By not rejecting [the gift], by being the object of the agent’s act of relinquishment, and by means of instigation or consent, one attains the status of a recipient (*sampradāna*). This is due to the distinction between the three types of operations that motivate the act of giving, as thus described.

Among these, the first is the deity and so forth; for example, "He gives *tulasī* to Nārāyaṇa," because there is no obstruction to the agent's activity due to the lack of any rejection [by the recipient]. The second is the beggar and so forth; for example, "He gives a cow to a Brāhmaṇa," because the agent is prompted by such requests as "Give! Give! The third, however, is the teacher and so forth; for example, "He gives his entire property to the teacher," because the prompting occurs through mere consent even in the absence of a formal request.

"Fixed," and so forth. That which, while not being the locus of the action expressed by the verbal root under discussion, is the locus of the disjunction produced thereby, is "fixed" (dhruva); and this, by implication, is the limit (avadhi). "Departure" (apāya) means separation, disjunction—that is to say, the destruction of a relation. Regarding "belonging to another": the state of being an *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure) consists in being the locus of the disjunction produced by an action, while not being the locus of that very action which produces the disjunction. Alternatively, it may be defined as follows.

Regarding *calam* (the moving): it has been stated by Hari—"That which remains indifferent (*udāsīna*) during a departure, whether it be moving or stationary, is regarded as the *apādāna* (ablative) because of its fixedness through connection (*āveśāt*). Here, the indifferent thing is the limit (*avadhi*). "Through connection" means through slight entry.

In the case of "from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt*), when a leaf brought by crows or other birds falls from another tree, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used because that [other] tree lacks the status of being a constituent part (*avayavatva*). However, when there is a relationship of part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used if one intends to express the relationship itself.

Regarding the term *adhikaraṇatva* (the state of being a locus): that in which actions (*kriyā*) are supported is called the *ādhāra* (locus). It is clear that this is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the action as mediated by the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*). That very thing is the *adhikaraṇa* (locus). On this point, it was stated by Hari: "That which, while not directly [supporting] the action, supports the action as mediated by the agent and the object, and assists in the accomplishment of the action, is designated as the *adhikaraṇa* in the grammatical treatise. (Vākyapadīya 3.7.142)

And that [locus] is fourfold—"The locus is fourfold by way of proximity (*sāmīpya*), contact (*śleṣa*), object (*viṣaya*), and pervasion (*vyāpti*)"—due to the fourfold nature of the distinguishing relations. Among these, the first example by way of the relation of proximity is: "A river is in the forest," and so forth; here, the forest and the like are the locus by way of the relation of proximity. The second is by way of the relation of partial contact (*ekadeśasaṃbandha*), as in: "He sits on a mat," and so forth; here, the mat and the like [are the locus].

The third [type of locus] is the locus by way of contact (*āśleṣa*), as in "there is a desire for liberation" (*mokṣe icchāsti*); here, liberation and so forth are the loci as objects (*viṣaya*). The fourth is by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*), as in "oil is in sesame seeds" (*tailaṃ tileṣu*); here, the sesame seeds and so forth are the loci as the pervaded (*vyāpya*).

Regarding the term "therein" (*tatra*): "compound-ness" (*samāsatva*) is the status of being a compound word through the relation of expressive power (*śakti*), or the state of being a collection of expressive powers that have attained a unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). This is based on the etymological derivation: "that which is compounded (*samas-yate*), joined together (*saṃśleṣyate*), and made into a single meaning (*ekārthīkriyate*). The resulting meaning is that compound-ness consists in being characterized by an indivisible attribute (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) that serves to establish the grammatical correctness of the words that produce the status of a single word for two or more constituent words. Furthermore, that compound is of six kinds. To illustrate: "A case-inflected word with another case-inflected word, a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) with a noun (*nāman*), a verbal root (*dhātu*), or a verbal suffix with a verbal suffix."

"The compound known as *subanta* is understood by the wise to be of six kinds" (Vaiśeṣika-sūtra-kārikā 28). Therein, the examples in order are as follows: 1. *Supāṃ supā* ("of case-endings with case-endings"): both words are *subanta* (ending in a case-suffix), as in *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"). 2. *Supāṃ tiṅā* ("of case-endings with verbal suffixes"): the first word is *subanta*, the latter is *tiṅanta* (ending in a verbal suffix), as in *paryabhūṣayat* ("he adorned completely"), and so forth. This is because of the Vārttika statement: "There is also a compound with a *tiṅ*-ending that possesses a prefix (*gati*) or an acute accent (*udāttavat*). 3. *Supāṃ nāmnā* ("of case-endings with a noun"): the first word is *subanta*, the latter is a noun (*nāman*), as in *kumbhakāraḥ* ("pot-maker"), and so forth.

The compound is formed by the rule stated as "upapadam atiṅ" (Pāṇini 2.2.19), according to the technical maxim (paribhāṣā): "gati-kāraka-upapadānāṃ kṛdbhiḥ samāsavacanaṃ prāk subutpatteḥ" (the statement regarding the compounding of gatis, kārakas, and upapadas with kṛt-derivatives occurs prior to the arising of case-endings). Thus, the compounding with the noun is established even before the case-endings arise; otherwise, in examples such as *carmakṛt*, the elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*) would be untenable. By the rule "supāṃ dhātunā," the subsequent member is merely a verbal root (*dhātu-mātra*) and not a finite verb ending in *tiṅ*.

For example: *kaṭaprūḥ* and so forth; this is a compound according to the Vārttika rule: "The suffix *kvip* is applied after the roots *vac*, *pracch*, *yat*, *stu*, *katapru*, and *juśrī*, and there is lengthening [of the vowel]. An example of one finite verb (*tiṅ*) with another finite verb is: *pibatakhādata* (drink and eat), *pacatamṛjyata* (cook and cleanse), and so forth; this is based on the rule included in the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group: "A finite verb may be compounded with another finite verb to express the continuity of an action."

An example of a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) with a nominal stem (*subanta*) is *jahistambhaḥ*. This compound is formed by the rule included in the *mayūravyaṃsaka* group: "In the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*), [a verb] is frequently compounded with its object and expresses the agent. This is the sixfold division of compounds. Regarding the term *ātman* (self): if it were dependent upon itself, there would be the undesirable consequence of circularity (*ātmāśraya*). That indeed occurs in three ways: through production, persistence, and cognition. For instance, if this state of being a compound were produced by the state of being a compound, then it would not exist subsequent to the moment that does not possess that state of being a compound.

If this "compound-ness" (*samāsatva*) were to reside in itself as compound-ness, then it would not be pervaded by that very compound-ness. If this compound-ness were non-different from the cognition of compound-ness (or non-different from the causal complex of the cognition), then it would be non-different from that compound-ness. This [inference] involves the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Therefore, it should be understood that there is no possibility [of such a relation] in any one of the types of compounds, such as *karmadhāraya*. As for the word "not" (*na*): the Naiyāyikas do not accept expressive power (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in a sentence; in their view, expressive power and indication reside only in the word (*pada*).

Regarding the phrase *dvigubhinne* and so forth: a *tatpuruṣa* compound consisting of words in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), excluding those that fall under the category of *dvigu*, is a *karmadhāraya*, according to the rule: "A *tatpuruṣa* with words in apposition is a *karmadhāraya*" (Pāṇini 1.2.42). Even there, because an exception (*apavāda*) is stronger than a general rule, the rule "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified" (Pāṇini 2.1.57) is more powerful. Thus, indeed, it is a *karmadhāraya*. Consequently, in that case, there is a collection of words possessing identical case-endings (*samānavibhaktimat-padakadambakatva*) and the capacity to convey non-difference (*abhedabodhakatva*).
This compound has the final member as its predominant element (*uttarapadapradhāna*).

Regarding the passage beginning with *niṣāda* and so forth: in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the meaning is understood through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the prior member; however, in a *bahuvrīhi*, it occurs in the final member. Furthermore, in a *dvandva* compound, since the intended meaning is established by the primary denotative power (*śakyārtha*) itself without resorting to metaphorical indication, there is no need at all to postulate such indication.

Regarding the term *tatpuruṣatvam*: it consists both in the primary denotation of the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) and, in this case, the facility of understanding the meaning of the final member through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of the prior member (*pūrvapada*). Although compounds such as *ardhakāya* lack that [facility], they nonetheless possess the status of a *tatpuruṣa* precisely because they are prescribed within that specific section by particular rules such as "the neuter [word] *ardha*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.2).

Regarding the term *dvigutvam* (the state of being a *dvigu*): it is the state of being a *tatpuruṣa* compound consisting of a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) preceded by a number that does not denote a conventional name (*saṃjñā*). The phrase "not denoting a conventional name" is included to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to compounds such as *pañcāmrāḥ* ("five mangoes"), which are *karmadhārayas* prescribed by the rule "In the case of names, [compounds of] direction and number [are *tatpuruṣas*]" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.50). The phrase "preceded by a number" is taken from the rule "A *tatpuruṣa* preceded by a number is a *dvigu*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.52), and is used to exclude cases such as *dvimūrdhaḥ* ("two-headed"), where the same technical designation would otherwise apply.

The state of being a *bahuvrīhi* consists in its denoting an object distinct from the meanings of the constituent words themselves. It is of two kinds: *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (where the subordinate member is included) and *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (where the subordinate member is not included). A *tadguṇa-bahuvrīhi* is one in which the meaning of a word that has become subordinate within the aggregate is understood as being connected with the whole aggregate; for example, in "Bring the long-eared one" (*lambakarṇam ānaya*), the ear (*karṇa*) is also connected with the act of bringing, because without it, the bringing of the subject itself would be impossible.

Or, since [the object] is brought only by way of its specific qualification when such a possibility exists, its connection lies in that which is being brought. That which is different from it is "devoid of its qualities" (*atadguṇa*). For instance, in expressions such as "bring the sea that has been seen," the sea itself cannot be brought; thus, it is of that nature [i.e., *atadguṇa*]. Furthermore, it is of two kinds: that composed of words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) and that composed of words in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Among these, an example of an appositional *bahuvrīhi* is "one whose garment is blue" (*nīlāmbara*), whereas in the case of a non-appositional compound, it is "staff-in-hand" (*daṇḍapāṇi*), and so forth.

"Dvandvatva" (the nature of a *dvandva* compound) consists in its denoting all the word-meanings as primary (*prādhānyena*). Here, "primacy" (*prādhānya*) means not having attained the status of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*) with respect to the meanings of the constituent parts. By this, there is no impossibility [of the definition] even when there is a mutual absence of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*). Furthermore, that *dvandva* is of two kinds, due to the distinction between the *itaretara* (mutual) and the *samāhāra* (collective). The state of being *itaretara* is the denotation of the referents of the nouns qualified by numbers such as duality (*dvitva*), etc., where the specific number has not been grasped. The state of being *samāhāra* is the denotation of such a number residing in the referents of the nouns.

Regarding the term *avyayībhāvatva*: it consists primarily in the denotation of the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapada*). In that case, the first member is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) and the second member is not an indeclinable; by virtue of these, the aggregate—being both indeclinable and non-indeclinable—is called *avyayībhāva*. As for the group beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu*, their status as *avyayībhāva* is due to being prescribed in that specific section, since it is accepted at the beginning of the treatise (*śāstra*) that all definitions of compound types are merely general (*prāyika*).

As it has been stated by the learned: "The statement that 'compound [formation] is fourfold' is merely a general rule; likewise, this other [classification] which concerns the predominance of the meaning of the first member and so forth is also [merely general]. (Bhūṣaṇasāra). The sense is that even the division characterized by the predominant cognition of the meaning of the first member and so forth is only approximate.

*Upakumbham* ("near the jar"): the sentence-meaning is "in the vicinity of the jar. *Nirdhāraṇam* ("selection/discrimination"): the state of the qualificand possessing a property that distinguishes it from others within its own class.

Regarding the phrase "in sequence": therein, the examples for genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*) follow in order. To illustrate: in the expression "Among men, the Kṣatriya is the hero," *kṣatriyatva* (the state of being a Kṣatriya) is the genus. In the expression "Among cows, the black cow has the most abundant milk," *kṛṣṇatva* (blackness) is the quality. In the expression "Among travelers, the chariot-riders are the fastest," rapid movement is the action. Regarding "blue" and so forth: as an example of the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*), we have "blue" and so on; here, the absolute non-connection of blueness with the lotus is excluded.

Regarding the passage beginning with "śaṅkha" (conch): in the statement "The conch is indeed white," there is an exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*); that is, the connection of whiteness with the conch is excluded [from being otherwise].

"Pārtha," and so forth. Regarding the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), as in "Pārtha alone is the archer," the quality of being a preeminent archer is excluded from objects other than Pārtha. Regarding "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*): the meaning of a pronominal is that which is delimited by a property characterized by being the delimitor of the object-domain of the speaker’s cognition, or that which is qualified by the mode of a cognition conducive to its own utterance; this is the referent of the word *saḥ* (he/that) in such expressions as "May he grant you the desired fruit."

Now, regarding the word *iva* and so forth: the capacity of *iva* should be understood as functioning in the sense of comparison (*upamā*), poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), sentence ornamentation (*vākyālaṅkāra*), and the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*). Among these, regarding comparison, it is stated that because of the Vārttika rule—"With *iva*, there is always a compound, and there is no elision of the case-ending"—there is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*) and no elision of the case-ending; this is also what is understood here, as it is said: for example, "Speech and meaning, as if joined together" (*vāgarthāviva saṃpṛktau*). Regarding poetic fancy, for example: "The face of the deer-eyed one shines like another full moon."

As an ornament for a sentence (*vākyālaṅkāra*), as in: “Who indeed will ever endure [it],” and so forth. As in the sense of slightness (*īṣadartha*), as in: “[Her face] was slightly turned away from her breasts,” and so forth. Regarding the rule beginning with *uddeśya* (the subject), etc.: here, indeed, because of the statement that “the case-ending and gender must be identical for the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*),” there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For instance, in cases such as “one tree becomes five boats,” gender, number, and so on, are not the governing factors (*atantratva*).

Regarding the word *tatra*: "indicative" (*dyotakatva*) means the capacity to convey the intended meaning (*tātparya*). An authority for the indicative nature of prefixes (*upasarga*) is as follows: "Prefixes such as *pra* and others are indicative, and likewise particles (*nipāta*) such as *ca* and others; [this is seen] just as the suffix *lakāra* is seen in the expression 'Hari and Hara are worshipped' (*upāsyete hariharau*). (Vaiśeṣika-sūtra-kārikā 42). For here, is the act of worship (*upāsanā*) the meaning of the prefix alone, or of the [prefix] qualified [by the root], or of the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone? It cannot be the first.

If that were the case, since this root—which is transitive by virtue of denoting a result residing in a locus other than its own [agent]—does not denote a result in the form of *upāsanā* (meditation), the *L*-suffix would not occur in the sense of the object (*karman*) derived from it. Nor is the second alternative [correct], because it is unnecessarily cumbersome (*gaurava*). As for the third, the status of being a *dyotaka* (indicator) is attained, because it serves to apprehend the intended meaning (*tātparya*); such is the sense.

Thus, in cases such as "Śiva is realized," "adorned," or "accepted," one must acknowledge that these [prefixes] possess a denotative function (*vācakatva*)—just like prepositions—in order to establish the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) in those respective senses of the root. It should be understood that they are thus indicative (*dyotaka*). Regarding "jhanatkāra" and so forth: while it is true that the sounds "jhanatkāra" and the like are perceived only after the falling has occurred, nevertheless, the sound "jhanatkāra" and so forth is also perceived even before the completion of the action of falling; with respect to that [prior perception], there is a correct immediate succession (*ānantarya*) in the aforementioned instances.

Regarding the passage beginning with *saṃsarge*: it is said that this non-existence of relation (*saṃsargābhāva*) is threefold. For it is stated: "Prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), likewise destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*)—thus, non-existence of relation is held to have attained a threefold nature."

The term *prasajya* means having brought about a connection—that is, having superposed [something]. Negation (*pratiṣedha*) occurs according to the maxim: "That which is connected [to something else] is negated. Thus, there is a negation only of that which has been superposed as a possibility; therefore, even in cases such as "there is no color in the air," the negation is understood by the particle *nañ* only after first superposing color upon the air. This is the distinction. Accordingly: "Where the affirmation is subordinate and the negation is primary, and where the negative particle is connected with the verb, that is *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation)."

Regarding *paryudāsa*: "That in which affirmation (*vidhi*) is primary and negation (*pratiṣedha*) is secondary, where the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the subsequent word—that is to be known as *paryudāsa*.
As for the example *ālabheta*: it means "one should sacrifice," that is, "one should kill.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of general rules" (*sāmānyena*) and so forth: here indeed is the rule concerning relative strength—"A general rule is a *utsarga* (default rule); a specific rule is an *apavāda* (exception); between a *utsarga* and an *apavāda*, the rule of the *apavāda* is stronger."

Regarding the passage beginning with *viśeṣeṇa* (by way of specification), etc.: because a specific injunction (*viśeṣavidhi*) is restricted to only one part [of a general rule], it lacks scope due to its non-establishment otherwise.

This is why it is said in the passage beginning with *ata eva* (for this very reason), etc. As it is stated in the *Kaumudī*: "The scriptural (ānuśravika) [means] is like the perceptible (dṛṣṭavat); it is characterized by impurity, decay, and excess," and so forth. "Impurity" (*aviśuddhi*) refers to the fact that sacrifices such as the Soma sacrifice involve the means of killing animals, seeds, and so on. As the venerable teacher Pañcaśikha said: "There is a slight admixture (*saṅkara*), there is a remedy (*parihāra*), and there is endurance of the consequences (*pratyavamarṣa*)."

"Minor commingling" (*svalpasaṅkara*) refers to the commingling of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) arising from the primary sacrifice, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, with a small amount of the *apūrva* arising from animal slaughter and other acts that cause harm. This [commingling] is "remediable," meaning it can be removed even by a minor expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*). However, if, through negligence, the expiation and so forth are not performed, then at the time of the ripening of karma, it will produce an even greater misfortune.

"Sapratyavamarṣaḥ" means that which exists together with *pratyavamarṣa*, that is, with forbearance (*sahiṣṇutā*). As it has been said by the learned: "For those who are virtuous, having plunged into the great lake of the nectar of heaven brought about by their store of merit, endure even a tiny spark of the fire of suffering produced merely by sin."

"But," and so forth. In the *Ekākṣarakoṣa* (the Treasury of Single Syllables), each individual phoneme possesses denotative power; thus, a mere illustration is provided: "The letter *a* is Vāsudeva, and the letter *ā* is the Grandfather (Brahmā); the letter *i* is said to be Kāma, and the letter *ī* is said to be Lakṣmī," and so on.

"Though it lacks the dewlap and so forth," and so on. Even though the dewlap and other such features are absent, "gavayatva" (the state of being a gavaya) consists in possessing many properties similar to those of a cow. For similarity (*sādṛśya*) is indeed the possession of a plurality of properties belonging to that [other object]. Although the dewlap and so forth do not exist in the gavaya, it nonetheless possesses a plurality of properties similar to those of a cow. Thus, a certain forest-dweller said to a villager: "That which is similar to a cow is denoted by the word 'gavaya'."
Then, when that very villager, having at some time observed a gavaya, determines "this is a gavaya," it is clear that this is precisely what is accomplished by the cognition of analogy (upamiti).

Regarding the passage beginning with *vyavahāreṇa* (by usage), Durga states: "The conventional usage of people is *vyavahāra*; therefore, one should understand that the application [of a grammatical rule] is established even for what has not been explicitly stated. Indeed, such a state of affairs is to be understood from the elision (*lopa*) of particles (*nipāta*), indeclinables (*avyaya*), prefixes (*upasarga*), case-roles (*kāraka*), tense (*kāla*), number (*saṅkhyā*), and so forth. An example of this is: *harītakyaḥ phalāni* ("the myrobalan fruits"). For here, the feminine gender is applied even to the fruits themselves. Another example is: *khalatikaṃ vanāni* ("the thickets are forests"), where the word for the forests ends in the singular number.

Even when words have the same meaning, a difference in gender and number is observed; for example: *āpaḥ* (feminine plural) and *jalam* (neuter singular), or *dārāḥ* (masculine plural), *kalatram* (neuter singular), and *bhāryā* (feminine singular). Regarding this, Durga says: "Those [words] used by Vedic scholars and those known to worldly people are exactly as they have been stated; however, their meanings are to be determined from common usage, for there is no comprehensive collection of them."

And as for the word *sa* (that): according to the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), that word is sixfold. For it is said: "The word may be primary (*mukhya*), indicative (*lākṣaṇika*), secondary (*gauṇa*), metaphorical (*aupacārika*), etymological (*yaugika*), or conventional-etymological (*yogarūḍha*); thus the word is declared to be sixfold. This applies in cases such as *prāsādīyati* ("he acts like a palace"). Padmanābha says: "For one who acts like a palace in a hut, and acts like a couch on a mere mat, even a lowly woman (*kulikā*) acts like an apsaras for him, provided he is of a contented nature."

Regarding the passage beginning with *ūnaviṃśati* and so forth: according to the statement in the lexicon (*koṣa*), "All words beginning with *viṃśati* always denote both the thing numbered (*saṅkhyeya*) and the number itself (*saṅkhyā*)," it should be understood that the word-forms for numbers such as *ūnaviṃśati* possess the denotative power (*śakti*) for both the object to be counted and the count itself, and they take the singular ending.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Sāramañjarī* composed by Śrī Āśubodha Vidyābhūṣaṇa.
